text.title: HIPAA BAA Vendor Checklist Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for hipaa-baa-vendor-checklist. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Every vendor touching PHI MUST have a signed BAA on file before any PHI is shared; the BAA MUST be countersigned and dated.
rule.rationale: The Privacy Rule permits disclosing PHI to a business associate only on the strength of satisfactory assurances captured in a written agreement, so the impermissible act is the disclosure itself: it occurs the moment data moves, and a BAA signed afterwards does not retroactively make it permitted. The failure mode is mundane rather than exotic, namely a vendor onboarded for a pilot, PHI flowing, and legal papering the relationship weeks later.

rule.statement: Checklist MUST include a current data-flow diagram showing every PHI surface the vendor touches; unmapped surfaces block the engagement.
rule.rationale: The Security Rule's risk analysis obligation covers all electronic PHI the entity creates, receives, maintains or transmits, and no risk can be assessed for a flow nobody has drawn. The surfaces that go unmapped are rarely the primary integration; they are log exports, support-tool access and backup copies that carry PHI incidentally, each of them a channel the agreement's controls were never written to cover.

rule.statement: BAA MUST require the vendor to notify the covered entity of any PHI breach within 60 calendar days (and contractually narrowed to 72 hours where possible).
rule.rationale: Sixty days is the vendor's regulatory ceiling, not a schedule the covered entity can plan around: the covered entity's own notification clock runs from discovery too, and where the vendor acts as its agent the vendor's discovery is imputed to it. A vendor that consumes its full statutory window leaves almost no time to investigate, assess and notify, which is why the window is narrowed by contract. HIPAA permits the narrowing but does not supply it.

rule.statement: Vendor MUST disclose every sub-processor handling PHI; the covered entity reserves the right to object before a new sub-processor is onboarded.
rule.rationale: HIPAA pushes the obligation downstream, since a subcontractor that creates or receives PHI on a business associate's behalf is itself a business associate and needs its own agreement, but nothing in the rule requires anyone to tell the covered entity who those subcontractors are. The risk is therefore real while the visibility is not, unless the contract creates it. GDPR's processor regime supplies the workable pattern: a named list plus a right to object before a new one is engaged.

rule.statement: BAA MUST grant the covered entity audit rights with reasonable notice — at least annually or after a security incident.
rule.rationale: HIPAA does not require audit rights in a BAA. The reason to insist on them is what the Privacy Rule does require: a covered entity that knows of a pattern of activity amounting to a material breach by its business associate must take reasonable steps to cure it or end the arrangement. That duty is unmeetable without any mechanism capable of producing the knowledge, and relying on the vendor's assurances is not an answer once an incident has happened.

rule.statement: BAA MUST require return or certified destruction of PHI on contract termination; if infeasible, contractual protections extend post-termination.
rule.rationale: Retained PHI is liability that outlives the commercial relationship: after termination there is no active contract manager, no invoice to withhold and often nobody at the vendor who remembers the data exists, yet a breach of it is still notifiable. The regulation already anticipates that return or destruction is sometimes infeasible, which is exactly why the fallback of extended protections and limited further use has to be written down in advance rather than argued at termination.

rule.statement: Vendor MUST encrypt PHI at rest and in transit using NIST-approved algorithms (FIPS 140-2 / 140-3).
rule.rationale: The Security Rule treats encryption as addressable rather than required, which is routinely misread as optional. The real lever sits in breach notification, which is triggered only by unsecured PHI, and PHI encrypted by the methods HHS recognises falls outside that definition. Pinning validated, NIST-approved algorithms is what makes a lost laptop or a misdirected backup an internal incident instead of a reportable breach with individual, HHS and possibly media notification.

rule.statement: If no PHI is in scope or HIPAA does not apply to the engagement, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Every control here is calibrated to one statutory definition of PHI and one regulator's enforcement posture. Applied where HIPAA does not reach it manufactures false assurance: the vendor signs a BAA-shaped document no authority enforces, while the regime that actually governs the data, whether GDPR or a national health law, imposes requirements the checklist never asks about.
